Malgré l'épuisement des pompiers français, aucun pompier belge n'est appelé en renfort : "On attend le feu vert des autorités locales" Une quinzaine de volontaires belges se tiennent prêts à intervenir en Gironde pour épauler leurs homologues français épuisés. - Publié le 27-07-2026 à 20h53 Au moins quinze pompiers volontaires belges sont sur le pied de guerre pour venir en aide aux pompiers épuisés en Gironde. "Nous collaborons avec une organisation de volontaires allemands. Eux disposent d'une cinquantaine de pompiers prêts à être envoyés, et nous sommes une quinzaine de Belges, mais nous n'avons pas encore été sollicités par les autorités locales", explique Yves De Vogelaere, membre du conseil d'administration de l'ASBL Era, qui rassemble les volontaires belges. En cas de demande, les volontaires belges et allemands seraient immédiatement mobilisables pour se rendre sur les zones sensibles. "Nous travaillerons main dans la main et pourrons épauler nos homologues français. Pourquoi n'avons-nous pas encore été appelés ? Je l'ignore. Les Français savent en tout cas que nous sommes disponibles à tout moment", ajoute-t-il. "Ils pourront nous assigner un village ou un quartier spécifique, et nous procéderons de zone en zone pour sécuriser les lieux." B-Fast pas sollicité à ce stade Les Allemands disposent de moyens logistiques considérables, dont des véhicules tout-terrain équipés de lances à incendie pour se déplacer rapidement sur les lieux sinistrés. Des capacités que la Belgique ne peut pas revendiquer. Côté aérien, notre pays ne dispose "que" d'un hélicoptère de la police fédérale, le "Bambi Bucket", capable de larguer 1000 litres d'eau. "À l'heure actuelle, les autorités françaises sollicitent des moyens — avions et hélicoptères bombardiers d'eau — dont la Belgique, et par conséquent B-Fast (Belgian First Aid and Support Team, NdlR), ne dispose pas", indique Florinda Baleci, porte-parole du SPF Affaires étrangères. "Si la demande d'assistance venait à évoluer, le Comité de planification de B-Fast examinera ces changements et, en concertation avec le Conseil de coordination, déterminera si B-Fast est en mesure d'y répondre." Pour rappel, B-Fast est l'équipe belge spécialisée dans l'aide urgente internationale. Lors de catastrophes majeures à l'étranger, des experts, du matériel ou des modules spécialisés peuvent être déployés pour renforcer les premières opérations de secours, avant que l'aide humanitaire ou le pays concerné ne prenne le relais. Dès les premières heures d'une crise, un pays sinistré ou une organisation internationale — comme l'Union européenne ou les Nations unies — peut solliciter l'intervention de B-Fast. Chaque mission fait l'objet d'une évaluation approfondie, afin de garantir la sécurité des équipes sur le terrain. De son côté, le président français Emmanuel Macron a demandé jeudi dernier l'activation du mécanisme de protection civile de l'Union européenne pour lutter contre les incendies. Deux hélicoptères, tchèque et slovaque, ont déjà été fournis. L'Espagne a formulé la même demande et a reçu quatre avions bombardiers d'eau en provenance de Grèce et d'Italie.

Ben Needham's mum Kerry warns Greek locals she 'isn't going anywhere' as she dismisses claim her son is dead in new Disney+ crime documentary Kerry believes Ben is still alive Kerry Needham, the mother of missing toddler Ben, has issued a stark warning to the residents of Kos in a brand new Disney+ documentary. The bereft mum and her own mother – Ben’s grandmother – appear in the streaming service’s new series 20/20 Britain’s Most Notorious Crime Investigations. And she is very quick to dismiss the police’s previous conclusion that Ben died in Greece aged 21 months. Kerry has said that without a body or remains there is no evidence that Ben, who vanished in 1991, is dead. Ben Needham: Lost in Paradise on Disney+ 20/20 Britain’s Most Notorious Crime Investigations dropped today (Thursday July 30, 2026) on Disney+. The episode about little Ben is the first in the six-part series. Called Ben Needham: Lost in Paradise, the documentary looks back at the lead up to Ben’s disappearance in Kos, and what has happened since. Kerry and her mum Christine explain the story right from the start. And it begins with Kerry returning to Kos last year. Looking out to sea, she admits: “I hate coming back here. It makes me shake, it makes me feel physically sick. Coming back here makes me relive that day.” The family had left a “very poor area” in Sheffield, England, and moved to Kos in the early 90s. Kerry has two brothers, Stephen and Danny, who initially relocated with Christine and their dad Eddie. Kerry stayed in England with Ben’s dad Simon Ward. But their flat was dingy, they were young and Kerry missed her family. So she and Ben moved out to Kos, too. The family had rented an olive grove and Eddie and Stephen began working on the renovation of a farmhouse nearby. Kerry got a job in a local hotel bar as a waitress, while Christine looked after Ben. On that fateful day, Christine and Ben headed to visit Eddie and Stephen at work. Ben was playing with his two Dinky toy cars outside the farmhouse door. But a short while later, Christine was unable to find him. “Eddie went across the field shouting his name but he wasn’t there,” Christine recalls in the documentary. Stephen had already left on his motorbike to go home for a shower. Assumptions he had taken Ben with him were wrong. Christine and Stephen went to the local police station to report Ben missing, though no one could find him. As viewers of Ben Needham: Lost in Paradise will see, what ensued has been almost a four-decade hunt for Kerry’s beloved son. What happened to Ben Needham? In their search for Ben, Kerry and Christine reveal how they were sent on a wild goose chase. A public appeal on a Greek television programme sparked a call from a prisoner in jail. The man insisted a local Roma traveller family had stolen Ben. Christine and Eddie tracked them down with an interpreter but they were met with vitriol from the community. Shock scenes in Ben’s episode of 20/20 Britain’s Most Notorious Crime Investigations show a man hiding something under a tea towel. He screams and threatens to shoot them dead. There have been hundreds of reports of sightings of Ben since 1991. Computer generated images have provided age progression pictures but he has never been found. In 2012, South Yorkshire Police launched a new inquiry into Ben’s disappearance. Officers returned to Kos and spent years conducting a full scale dig and investigation in the area where he vanished. Officers concluded that Ben died in a digger accident. Did Konstantinos ‘Dino’ Barkas kill Ben Needham? Four years after the inquiry was launched, the police made a breakthrough. A witness claimed Ben had been playing close to where digger driver Konstantinos ‘Dino’ Barkas was driving his massive piece of machinery. The witness said he saw Dino on the following days and said he was “red, upset and sweating and in quite a state”. Detective Superintendent Matt Fenwick adds in the Disney+ documentary: “Dino said, ‘I ran over something that yelped and I thought it was a dog’.” Dino, who died in 2015, was said to have buried Ben’s body that same day. An excavation of an olive grove later recovered one of Ben’s Dinky cars. Forensic evidence on the toy car found it had been in contact with blood or tissue that had decomposed. DS Fenwick says: “You’re left with the one plausible explanation. I think that Dino went into the area where Eddie was doing the renovation. Ben was playing between the two properties. “I think it’s likely that Ben came onto contact with that huge piece of machinery. I think Ben died as a result of that.” DS confirms in the documentary that believes it was an accident. He thinks Ben’s body was moved by Dino in a bid to cover up his crime. Dino’s family, however, vehemently deny South Yorkshire Police’s theory. And there’s a twist. Kerry Needham issues warning to Kos locals Two years after the car was found, Kerry received a phone call. It came following advances in DNA testing. She tearfully recalls in the Disney+ documentary: “They said, ‘Kerry, I’m sorry to tell you but the human decomposition inside the car, it’s not a match to Ben’s’. “I was thinking, why are you sorry? Because that means he’s alive. It means the accident didn’t happen. “You didn’t find his body or anything else. All you found was a toy car. So he’s not dead then.” Kerry vows to never stop looking for her little boy. In a very stark warning to the people of Kos, she says: “Ben is still a missing person in my mind. We as a family will never let this lie. “I appeal to those people on Kos to tell me the truth, tell me what happened. Tell me where he is if you can and I will go away. “But until then, I’m not going anywhere.”

U.S. President Donald Trump’s announcement that he had canceled another large-scale strike on Iran after the outlines of a possible agreement were reached caught Israelis at the height of the summer travel season, when airports, vacations and overseas flights are at their busiest. Yet while the Israeli public continues to endure daily uncertainty over whether the country could be drawn deeper into the confrontation with Iran, the government has again remained silent, apparently wary of being portrayed internationally as the side pushing for war. The silence continued even after Trump said Israel had joined his commitment to refrain from military action. “The country of Israel joins me in this commitment,” Trump wrote on Truth Social after announcing that he had agreed to cancel the planned attack, provided that a deal could be reached quickly. There was no immediate public confirmation from Jerusalem. Trump’s decision marked the latest sharp shift in a policy that has veered for nearly four months between threats of overwhelming military force and efforts to cool the confrontation. Iranian officials were quick to mock the reversal. “Trump retreated again,” Mohammad Marandi, a senior Iranian figure associated with the regime’s negotiating delegation, wrote on X shortly after the announcement. The central issue driving the latest escalation, freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, remains unresolved. Iran continues to oppose unrestricted passage through the strategic waterway without its approval, and no clear solution appears imminent. The strait is a critical energy route through which a significant share of Gulf oil and gas exports reaches global markets. Weeks of U.S. strikes against Iranian military targets have failed to restore secure maritime traffic. The campaign against Iran has now entered its sixth month, leaving Israel and the wider region in prolonged uncertainty. Only days earlier, Trump had said from Camp David that the United States was still considering further military action and warned that Washington could “hit them very hard.” It remained unclear what would ultimately determine whether he ordered another attack. The heightened tension prompted the U.S. State Department to issue security warnings Saturday. American embassies in 11 countries across the region, including Israel, urged U.S. citizens to consider leaving or prepare for a rapid departure in the event of escalation. Trump said Sunday morning that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked Washington to refrain from attacking. “The U.S.A. is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II,” he wrote. “Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to.” Trump said the emerging understandings would include the “immediate, complete, and total opening” of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to the Iranian nuclear threat. “Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the world and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a deal,” he wrote. “Get to work, everybody, and get it done.” No additional details have been released on the terms under discussion, the timetable for negotiations or the concessions expected from either Washington or Tehran. The announcement came after reports that Trump was seriously considering broad strikes against Iranian energy facilities and infrastructure. U.S. officials had said no final order had been issued, but the option was under active consideration following an Iranian attempt to strike an American base in Jordan and continued disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly played a central role behind the scenes in trying to prevent the attack. According to reports, he warned Trump that U.S. strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure could trigger retaliation against oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Pakistan also worked in recent days to promote de-escalation and revive negotiations. Iran, meanwhile, warned that any new American or Israeli attack would draw a forceful response. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi threatened that Tehran could target energy facilities and infrastructure in Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. Those threats intensified fears that another strike would not remain confined to Iran but could ignite a much broader regional confrontation. Senior Iranian officials told The New York Times that Tehran had used the ceasefire to prepare a plan for activating its proxies and intensifying attacks on U.S. allies, with the aim of imposing the heaviest possible military and economic cost on Trump. Elements of that strategy appeared to have surfaced last week, when two liquefied natural gas storage tankers, including one under American ownership, caught fire after a drone attack near the Suez Canal. Saudi Arabia later joined the United States in airstrikes against pro-Iranian militias in Iraq, which were suspected of attacking Saudi oil installations. The latest uncertainty has immediate consequences for ordinary Israelis. Families waiting in lines at Ben Gurion Airport, planning summer vacations or simply trying to get through the school break now face the constant possibility that flights could be canceled, Israeli airspace could close or a broader war could erupt. The repeated policy reversals in Washington have turned that uncertainty into a logistical nightmare. For now, Israelis are again left learning about the “outlines of a deal” from the U.S. president while wondering how stable those understandings are, whether Iran will reopen the Strait of Hormuz and what Trump’s latest reversal will ultimately mean for Israel’s security.

Published July 29, 2026 RAWALAKOT: Law enforcement agencies continue operations against armed groups carrying out attacks against security personnel in Azad Jammu and Kashmir's (AJK) Rawalakot, a top police official said on Wednesday. Addressing a press conference in Rawalakot, AJK police spokesperson, Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Khawar Ali Shaukat, said that armed attackers have taken positions in different buildings across the city. His remarks come amid violent clashes in the city involving supporters of the proscribed Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) amid general elections in the region. The AJK government had declared JAAC a proscribed organisation on June 5 under the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA), accusing the group of involvement in terrorism. The ban was imposed days before the committee's planned June 9 protest demanding the abolition of 12 AJK Assembly seats reserved for refugees from Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir (IIOJK) who migrated to Pakistan after 1947. During today's presser, SSP Shaukat said that armed groups continue carrying out attacks on law enforcement personnel in different areas, adding that no concession would be given to "miscreant elements". According to the official, at least one Rangers personnel was martyred in the attacks as enforcement agencies continue operations against the armed groups. The AJK police spokesperson said that police arrested several miscreants during the ongoing operations and recovered sophisticated weapons. Terming the attacks on security forces and state institutions "unacceptable", he maintained that state institutions had consistently exercised restraint. Those involved in attacks against state institutions would be dealt with "with an iron hand", he said. SSP Shaukat said that the "links" of the miscreants extended elsewhere and claimed that anti-state elements were spreading negative propaganda on social media. He vowed that authorities would not allow peace in the region to be undermined. The federal government has termed the violence involving the banned JAAC an attempt to disrupt the ongoing electoral process and undermine peace in the region. State Minister for Interior Talal Chaudhry on Tuesday said that the federal government would fully support the AJK administration to crush agitators. Speaking at a press conference in Islamabad alongside Federal Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, the minister said that the banned outfit's campaign was "not a movement to secure rights, but one aimed at taking rights away from the people". He alleged that the proscribed group was seeking to deprive Kashmiris of their right to vote and undermine the democratic process. The first phase of the AJK elections was held on July 27, with Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) securing victory in nine constituencies, according to unofficial and provisional results. Polling was held across all 13 constituencies in Mirpur, Kotli and Bhimber districts. According to the unofficial results, the PML-N won nine seats, while the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) secured four.

Corey Ruiz's sister said her brother's criminal record should not define him, as she delivered an emotional plea for justice during a news conference attended by family members and supporters following his fatal shooting by police. Ruiz, 38, was fatally shot by a Madison police officer on Wednesday after officers responded to reports of a man allegedly threatening people with a knife near East Washington Avenue and North First Street. According to the Madison Police Department, Ruiz refused repeated commands to drop the knife and injured one officer during a struggle before another officer opened fire. Authorities have said one officer sustained non-life-threatening injuries. The Wisconsin Department of Justice's Division of Criminal Investigation is leading an independent investigation into the shooting, while the officers involved have been placed on administrative leave. The family's appearance came as protests over Ruiz's death continued to grow in Madison, with demonstrators demanding accountability and greater transparency from city officials. Ruiz's sister said her brother's past should not overshadow the circumstances of his death and that his criminal record did not define him. Newsweek contacted Madison police Saturday via email for comment. 'His Criminal Record Does Not Define Who My Brother Was' Fighting back tears, Ruiz's sister began by thanking those who had rallied around the family. "I just want to thank the community and everyone that is standing up to support my family and my brother as we fight for justice for his execution," she said. Visibly moved, she continued: "There has already been so much negativity about him, and nobody even knows who he is. His criminal record tells a tale of trauma, of pain, of struggle. It does not define who my brother was." Supporters standing nearby responded with words of encouragement, with one person calling out, "That's right." Claims of 'Execution' Questioning the circumstances surrounding the shooting, she said: "And for him to be executed the way he was based on, in conclusion, based on speculation... I don't understand. I need somebody to help me understand why they felt it was okay to execute my brother." As she paused to wipe away tears, another supporter shouted, "It wasn't." She then added: "Based on no facts at all." After lowering her head during a prolonged pause, while relatives and supporters comforted her, she continued: "Why is it the police's decision to decide that he gets to pay an alleged debt to society with his life?" Solemn Gathering Overcome with emotion, she wrung her hands as members of the crowd called out "take your time" and offered further words of support. During the pause, a man standing beside her told those gathered she had driven through the night from Austin, Texas, after learning what had happened to her brother. Others standing alongside her appeared solemn, with some consoling one another and others visibly holding back tears. Resuming her remarks, she urged those who believed the shooting was justified to reflect on their views. "Everybody that feels like this was justified, I need you to check in with your higher power," she said, before adding while shaking her head, "because we've got some more stuff coming." She concluded by calling for continued public support as the family seeks accountability. "I hope everyone continues to support and come together and help us find justice for him, some kind of peace for us knowing that this murderer is not able to do this to somebody else," she said. As the news conference ended, the man standing beside her, civil rights attorney Ben Crump, repeatedly chanted, "Justice for Corey!" with others in attendance echoing the call. Ruiz's death has sparked days of demonstrations across Madison, with hundreds of protesters gathering at the scene of the shooting before marching through downtown and to the Wisconsin State Capitol. Demonstrators have called for accountability, the release of additional information about the shooting and justice for Ruiz. Flowers, candles and handwritten messages have also been left at a growing memorial near the site where he was killed. Protests have also disrupted official events. A city news conference was repeatedly interrupted by demonstrators demanding answers from Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and Police Chief John Patterson, while an outdoor concert planned at the Capitol was canceled amid the unrest. Local news station WMTV15 reported that protestors were continuing to gather on and around Williamson Street, where sections of the road are closed off with trucks and barriers, and some businesses in the area have decided to close, whilst many others remain open in a show of solidarity. “I feel like the best way for us to serve our community, especially with the resources we have, being like the physical space as well as like the proximity, we’re able to support our community this way,” Taylor Swanson, General Manager of Gib’s store said, as per the outlet. As reported by Newsweek, the Ruiz family has retained civil rights attorney Crump, who has called for criminal charges against the officer who fired the fatal shots. Crump has argued the force used against Ruiz was excessive, while police have maintained the shooting was justified because Ruiz allegedly wounded an officer with a knife during the encounter. The case has also renewed scrutiny of the Madison Police Department's lack of body-worn cameras. Because officers were not equipped with body cameras during the incident, investigators are relying on bystander video, surveillance footage and witness accounts to reconstruct what happened. The Wisconsin Department of Justice has said its investigation remains ongoing. Once complete, its findings will be turned over to the Dane County District Attorney's Office, which will determine whether any criminal charges are warranted. Ruiz's Extensive Criminal History Ruiz had an extensive criminal history. Court records reviewed by Newsweek show he had been in and out of jail over the past decade. He had prior convictions for misdemeanor retail theft and resisting or obstructing an officer in 2024. A year earlier, he was convicted of battery or threat to a judge, prosecutor or law enforcement officer, a felony, records show. In 2021, Ruiz had been convicted of resisting an officer with substantial bodily harm, a felony, according to Wisconsin court records. Ruiz also had prior convictions for felony cocaine and marijuana possession in 2014, as well as misdemeanor disorderly conduct in 2007. Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.

The Ministry of National Defense yesterday said it is monitoring the construction of full-scale replicas of military and government sites in Taiwan by the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA). The comments from ministry spokesman Major General Sun Li-fang (孫立方) come after a report by the Telegraph on satellite imagery showing replicas of Taiwan’s Presidential Office Building, Suao Naval Base and other sites. Citing satellite imagery and defense analysts, the report, published on Sunday, said that the PLA had built life-size replicas of key government facilities to rehearse military operations under realistic conditions. Photo: Screen grab from Google Earth The report described the scale and specificity of the training facilities as “unprecedented.” China had constructed replicas of Yokosuka Naval Base in Japan, which has the largest US naval base in that country, and Suao Naval Base in Yilan County, it said. Satellite imagery showed a mock-up of a Keelung-class destroyer berthed inside the replica of the Suao base, it said. Reports of PLA mock-up facilities have surfaced several times in the past few years. Satellite imagery first showed replicas of US aircraft carriers and destroyers in China’s northwestern deserts in 2021, while analysts in 2024 identified life-size replicas of Taipei’s Boai Special Zone, including the Presidential Office Building, at a military base in Inner Mongolia. More recent imagery has shown mock-ups of the Suao base and the Yokosuka base, which analysts say could be used to rehearse strikes against key military and government targets in a Taiwan contingency. Asked about the report, Sun said the military has “a comprehensive understanding” of the PLA’s construction of the replicas through its intelligence-gathering efforts. The armed forces have consistently planned for all possible scenarios involving Chinese military action against Taiwan and developed contingency measures, he said. “The disclosure of this information reminds us that the threats we face today are extremely serious,” Sun said, adding that the ministry takes the developments seriously and would continue strengthening force development, combat readiness and military training. He called on the public to support the ministry’s annual and special defense budgets to ensure it has the resources needed to maintain combat readiness. F-16 REIMBURSEMENTS Separately, a National Audit Office report on the central government’s final accounts for last year said that Taiwan is entitled to reimbursement from other countries’ purchasing systems developed under the air force’s F-16A/B upgrade program because it independently funded development of key subsystems. As of the end of October last year, the US had either disbursed or was reviewing reimbursement payments of more than US$245.23 million, the report said. Responding to the report, Sun said the air force had already explained to the National Audit Office that US foreign military sales regulations cap such reimbursements. For the F-16 program, the reimbursement ceiling is US$319 million, and Taiwan has already received about US$245 million in research and development cost-sharing payments, he said. The air force will continue to monitor other countries’ participation in the program through project management meetings and regular meetings and videoconferences with US officials to ensure Taiwan receives the reimbursement to which it is entitled, Sun said. ‘GRAY ZONE’ TACTICS: It was the first time a PLA chopper had crossed the line and could be part of training maneuvers in an invasion scenario, a researcher said The Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) sent a helicopter across the median line of the Taiwan Strait to traverse a restricted flight zone east of the line for the first time on Monday, introducing two new “gray zone” tactics in a single day, a researcher said yesterday. By Tarek Anthony oregonlive.com SALEM, Ore. — More than 1 million acres continued to burn across Oregon on Tuesday as firefighters took advantage of a rare stretch of thunderstorm-free weather to battle dozens of active wildfires across the state. | BETTER EVERY SHIFT: Fennessy’s vision for the future of wildfire response Here is an update on the largest fires burning statewide: Bench fire The Bench and Beachcomb fires merged into a single, fast-growing blaze that had burned more than 45,000 acres on the Warm Springs Indian Reservation in central Oregon by Tuesday. The fire destroyed six homes and five other structures Sunday night into Monday, fueled by strong winds, officials said. Strong winds Monday pushed the fire across both sides of the Deschutes River and Lake Billy Chinook, driving it toward more populated areas and threatening multiple communities on the Warm Springs Reservation. Level 3 (go now)evacuation orders remain in effect across much of the reservation north of Lake Billy Chinook and west of Madras. Officials have opened shelters for residents at the Old School Cafeteria in Warm Springs and St. Patrick Catholic School in Madras. A large-animal shelter remains open at the Jefferson County Fairgrounds in Madras. Pacific Power shut off electricity at three locations on the reservation, affecting fewer than 50 residents. Crews battled 90-degree heat and strong winds Monday as officials warned there was a “high potential” for further fire growth. Rowe Creek complex More than 1,300 personnel are battling the Rowe Creek complex, which encompasses nearly a dozen fires across central Oregon and is anchored by the roughly 71,000-acre fire formerly known as the Brewer fire east of Madras. The Brewer fire merged Monday with the Green Mountain and Crosswhite fires, bringing the combined burn area to more than 294,000 acres. The merged blaze is now known as the Rowe Creek complex-west zone. Officials have closed more than 20 miles of U.S. 26 east of Prineville, from milepost 34.8 to milepost 66, because of fire activity. The highway is a key route connecting Prineville and John Day and beyond into Idaho. Crews are focused on protecting homes east of Prineville, including in the Mill Creek, Johnson Creek and Marks Creek areas. Evacuation orders remain in effect across large portions of Crook and Jefferson counties, though relatively few residents are affected. Operations Chief Rob Hutchens said crews received two additional firefighting crews from California on Tuesday morning as firefighters continued efforts to protect homes along the southern edge of the fire. Air quality also remained a concern across the Prineville area Tuesday with Air Quality Index readings measuring at 152 out of 500 — considered to be unhealthy for sensitive groups. The blaze is 33% contained. Akawa Butte fire The lightning-caused Akawa Butte fire continues to burn more than 27,000 acres north of Sisters. Despite hot, breezy conditions Monday, crews made progress extinguishing hot spots and clearing lingering heat up to 100 feet inside the fire line. Operations Chief Cody Lokan said Tuesday morning that crews had contained the northeastern corner of the fire, which had been burning on remote public land. Operations Chief Steve Chapman said crews would remain focused Tuesday on cleaning up burned material in the fire’s southwestern area, where homes are most concentrated. Chapman said firefighters use water and hand tools to mix burning material into what crews call a “mud pie” to ensure it does not reignite. “It’s kind of like being a kid sometimes, so it’s kind of fun,” Chapman said. Oregon State Fire Marshal teams will spend their last night on the fire Tuesday, Chapman said, as crews begin transitioning cleanup efforts back to wildland firefighters. Officials will hold a community meeting at Sisters High School at 6:30 p.m. Tuesday to provide residents with the latest updates. Teen killer appears to boast about murder in rap video filmed inside prison , 19, was given a life sentence last week after being found guilty of killing the 16-year-old on a North Ayrshire beach in 2025 A teenager convicted of murdering Kayden Moy has shared footage online from behind bars seemingly bragging about the killing. Jay Stewart, 19, received a life sentence last week following his conviction for the murder of the 16 year old on a North Ayrshire beach in 2025. The two-minute mobile phone clip was recorded inside a cell at HMP Polmont, showing Stewart with a t-shirt covering his face while rapping about the murder, and seemingly threatening additional violence following his eventual release. Responding to the footage on Thursday, Kayden's father Paul stated: "Today my family was devastated by a leaked video from inside Polmont showing Jay Stewart convicted of killing my son singing, laughing, and appearing to boast about taking my son's life. "Nothing will ever prepare a parent for something like this. "We live every day with the heartbreak of losing Kayden while the person responsible appears to show no remorse and no respect." The clip was recorded on a phone held by another prisoner, who can be heard laughing and cheering at several moments. The profanity-filled verses contain numerous references to the killing of "KM" or "Kayden". He also seemingly threatens additional violence upon release, stating at one point: "Everyone knows my scheme is violent, big plan for future ahead." Stewart and Cole Turley, 18, both received minimum 16-year prison sentences for the murder, while a 15 year old boy was imprisoned for a minimum of 14 years. Kayden suffered fatal stab wounds on Irvine beach on May 17. On the day of the incident, the teenagers travelled by train to Irvine, carrying a lock-back knife and a cosh concealed within clothing and a rucksack. After an initial altercation at the beach, the teenagers pursued Kayden, inflicting the fatal wound after he stumbled and fell to the ground. Subsequently, they were filmed on camera seemingly celebrating the attack. A Scottish Prison Service spokesperson said: "We understand the lasting impact this kind of offending has on families and the significant distress such videos can cause. "Our staff work hard to keep prisons safe and secure, using all available technology and intelligence to prevent illicit items, including mobile phones, entering our establishments. "While we do not comment on individuals, we continue to work with Police Scotland, and other partners, to take action against those who attempt to breach our security." A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Inquiries are ongoing following a report of an online communication offence from HM YOI Polmont on Tuesday July 28 2026."

ALLEN TWP., Pa. -- The Philadelphia Police Commissioner is responding to the arrest of one of his officers for a shooting in Northampton County. That officer was off duty at the time, and he's now charged with homicide in the killing of his own uncle. It was just before 2 p.m. Friday when shots rang out in a house on Old Gate Rd. in Allen Township. 25-year-old Philadelphia Police Officer Kenroy Cummings is accused of shooting and killing his own uncle, 27-year-old Shakair Moncrieffe. The police report said one of Cummings' younger relatives called him to the house because Moncrieffe was threatening the boy. It was a shock to John Sousa and Jerry Caliendo, who live on the same street. "I was at work at the time, and my daughter texted me because she heard about it. Then my other daughter texted me to make sure I was alright, see if I was home," said Sousa. "They roped off the whole area for the day and the next day, when nobody could get their car out," said Caliendo. It was also shocking for Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel. "It's a tragedy when we have a police officer taking the life of someone, and so we're investigating that matter," said Bethel. Investigating how a respected member of the force for several years got involved in something like this. "Two years, from all indications I get, he was a good police officer here," said Bethel. "We train our men and women in deescalation. We train our men and women not to use deadly force." But Cummings admitted to using deadly force on his uncle, shooting him six times in the head and once in the wrist, according to court records. Cummings told police it was self-defense, because Moncrieffe was going for Cummings' gun, but Bethel said whatever the backstory is, it will likely end with Cummings losing his badge. "Over the next period of time, we'll go through a process where we will start to move him and remove him from the police department. Dismiss him from the police department," said Bethel. It's a story Sousa is still trying to fully understand. "A cop being involved in something like this? I mean that's crazy. You look to those people to protect and serve, not to perpetrate something like this," said Sousa.

Oregon prison officer indicted for harassing, cyberstalking ex-girlfriend on Facebook PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - An officer with the Oregon Department of Corrections has been indicted on charges of cyberstalking his ex-girlfriend from January 2024 to October 2024, the U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Oregon, announced on Thursday. According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, 46-year-old Jack Daniel Rowlett set up fake social media profiles on Facebook which he used to post “offensive and degrading claims about the victim.” Those included false claims about the woman’s sexual history with the men depicted in the fake accounts, according to the U.S. attorney. Those posts caused “significant emotional distress and reputational harm.” The woman tried to get a protective order against Rowlett for making the harassing posts, but Rowlett fought the order and denied responsibility for the accounts. After a federal investigation, Rowlett was allegedly linked to those posts that he denied responsibility for. On Thursday, Rowlett was arraigned in federal court, where he pleaded not guilty and was ordered released pending further court proceedings. According to the U.S. attorney, the Oregon Department of Corrections cooperated in the investigation. When reached for comment, the Oregon Department of Corrections told FOX 12 that Rowlett is employed at the Columbia River Correctional Institution in Portland, but has been on administrative leave. However, the DOC said he is now being moved to unpaid leave pending a personnel hearing on the matter: “At the Oregon Department of Corrections (DOC), employees are expected to uphold the highest standards of integrity and professionalism. These expectations are reflected in the department’s Code of Conduct and are essential to maintaining the public’s trust. “When allegations of employee misconduct arise, the department takes them seriously. We work closely with our law enforcement partners to ensure allegations of criminal conduct are thoroughly investigated,” the DOC said in a statement. In response to FOX 12 questions, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Rowlett was working at the Coffee Creek Correctional Facility, Oregon’s only women’s prison, when his relationship with the victim began. US Marshals arrest 61 fugitives, clear 97 felony warrants during central Iowa operation A four-day operation led by the U.S. Marshals Service resulted in the arrests of 61 wanted fugitives and the clearance of 97 felony arrest warrants across central Iowa, according to federal officials. The U.S. Marshals Service's Southern Iowa Fugitive Task Force coordinated the multi-agency operation called "Operation Heatwave" with state, local and federal law enforcement agencies aimed at locating and arresting dangerous fugitives throughout the region. Officials said planning and target identification began on June 29, with enforcement taking place from July 21-24. Authorities said the operation focused on violent offenders and gang members wanted for crimes including homicide, robbery, sexual assault, aggravated assault, weapons offenses and other serious felony crimes. Among the notable arrests highlighted by the U.S. Marshals Service: - Alfred Pyne, 18, was arrested July 21 in Urbandale on warrants from the Urbandale Police Department alleging intimidation with a dangerous weapon and reckless use of a firearm. Officials said the charges stem from a shooting at Urbandale's Lions Park during the city's Fourth of July celebration. - Kristopher Keys, 28, was arrested July 21 in Des Moines on multiple Iowa Department of Public Safety warrants for possession of a controlled substance, possession of a firearm by a felon and tampering with a witness. - Jacob Kerr, 26, was arrested July 21 in West Des Moines on a Polk County probation violation warrant tied to convictions for possession of a firearm by a felon and operating while intoxicated. He also was wanted on a Dallas County probation violation warrant related to a conviction for pimping or procuring for prostitution. - Chad Smith, 44, was arrested July 24 in Des Moines on a warrant for second-degree sexual abuse. He had been a fugitive since the 2024 sexual assault of a juvenile female. According to the U.S. Marshals, Smith was found by an Iowa State Patrol K-9 while hiding in a "void specifically designed to conceal his location." The U.S. Marshals Service said Operation Heatwave was part of a coordinated effort to remove dangerous fugitives from communities across central Iowa. Officials did not identify all of the agencies involved in the operation.

THE ASAHI SHIMBUN July 27, 2026 at 16:18 JST SAGAMIHARA, Kanagawa Prefecture--Mourners gathered at a care facility here on July 26 to mark the 10th anniversary of a stabbing rampage that killed 19 disabled residents, an attack that has fueled calls for a prejudice-free society. The mass murder at the Tsukui Yamayurien care home, which left 26 others injured, was committed by a former employee who expressed resentment against disabled people. He has been sentenced to death. Throughout the day, a steady stream of visitors laid flowers at a stone memorial monument and prayed for the victims and for a more inclusive world. The names of 11 of the 19 people killed are engraved on the monument. Among the visitors was a 62-year-old woman, accompanied by her 31-year-old son, who came to remember her daughter, Miho, who was murdered at age 19. At the monument, the mother traced the name “Miho” with her finger and laid down a bouquet of sunflowers. “Miho, I’m here. I’m so glad so many people have come and are remembering you,” the woman said. Kazuya Ono, 53, a former Tsukui Yamayurien resident who was seriously wounded in the attack, arrived with his caregiver, Yasuki Otsubo, 58. Ono, who now lives independently in an apartment, had once been unable to approach the site of his trauma. For each of the last three years, however, he has returned to the facility to pay his respects. A PLEA FOR ACCEPTANCE For Yukio Tachibana, 76, it was his first visit. The retired truck driver from Hachioji, western Tokyo, said he used to see Tsukui Yamayurien residents walking outside the facility on his routes. After retiring, he began driving for a disability facility transport service, where he said he still witnesses the depth of parental love every day. “Socially vulnerable people also have a right to live. I hope for a society that can be gentle and supportive,” he said. A 22-year-old university student from Chiba Prefecture, who uses a wheelchair due to cerebral palsy, recalled the anguish she felt as a 12-year-old when she learned about the attack. “I was shocked that people in the same situation as me had their lives taken,” she said. “I felt that I was on the side being rejected.” She voiced fears that prejudice against people with disabilities is spreading in Japan. “I want people to never forget this incident and to keep thinking about it,” she urged. Yuko Nosaku, a 49-year-old office worker from Yokohama, came to the site with her husband and their 13-year-old son, Sota, who has Down syndrome. She explained that the emotional toll of the attack had been so great that she was unable to visit the memorial until now. Her chest tightens, she said, whenever she sees online comments calling for the exclusion of people with disabilities. “I want this to become a society where my son can live easily, just like everyone else,” she said. TWISTED BELIEF The attack was one of the deadliest mass murders committed by a single perpetrator in postwar Japan. And the motive added to the heinousness of the crime. The massacre was carried out in the early hours of July 26, 2016, by Satoshi Uematsu, then 26, who broke into the facility where he had previously worked for over three years. The Yokohama District Court in March 2020 sentenced Uematsu to death, noting that he had developed a twisted belief that severely disabled people who cannot communicate are an “unnecessary presence” and “bring misery to their families and those around them.” His death sentence was finalized after he withdrew an appeal. He has since requested a retrial twice. His second request was dismissed in February, and he is currently appealing that decision. U.S. Attorney Leah Foley said the Department of Justice isn’t targeting Massachusetts by sending election monitors to two Bay State cities in September. “This is not a news story, for anyone to suggest that Massachusetts is getting targeted by this DOJ for any inappropriate reason is just false,” Foley said Sunday during and interview on WCVB’s On the Record. Federal monitors, which are set to go to Boston and New Bedford, are also being sent to jurisdictions in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, and Virginia to oversee primary elections. The DOJ has said monitors are a part of an effort to increase voter confidence and voting accuracy, something Foley agrees with. “We’re not doing it to smear the state of Massachusetts,” she said. Monitors have been sent to Massachusetts “numerous times throughout numerous administrations,” she said, adding that monitors are sent to different locations throughout the country and that she’d previously worked as a monitor in Louisiana after Katrina. “Trying to make sure that elections are conducted with integrity should not be controversial,” Foley said. Asked if voter fraud was an issue in the Commonwealth, Foley replied, “Whether it’s a problem or not, I don’t think there is any evidence to suggest that it’s a rampant problem in Massachusetts.” “But,” she continued, “as federal officials, we have the obligation to ensure that the public has the confidence that our elections are run competently and with integrity.” Foley also spent a portion of the Sunday interview discussing immigration and Trump administration policies, declining to comment on cases or incidents that happened outside of her district, including the fatal shooting of a man in Maine by an ICE officer. “It was not in our jurisdiction and therefore I have no information about what happened,” she said. “One of the things I believe which churns this discontent across the country are people assuming facts, and when something serious happens, you can’t assume the facts,” she added, telling WCVB that it was inappropriate to comment on incomplete investigations and ones she doesn’t have the facts for. “I don’t speculate because to do so is highly irresponsible,” she said. Foley also declined to comment on the investigations into ex-FBI Director James Comey or New York Attorney General Letitia James, citing the same reasons.

AYRSHIRE'S four MPs have urged the Scottish Government to pass on business rates reductions announced by the UK Government to pubs, social clubs and live music venues across Scotland. In a joint letter to Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth, they called for the Scottish Government to match both the 15 per cent business rates reduction introduced in England this year and the further 20 per cent reduction announced by Prime Minister Andy Burnham from April 2027. The MP's - Central Ayrshire's Alan Gemmell, North Ayrshire & Arran's Irene Campbell, Ayr Carrick and Cumnock's Elaine Stewart and Kilmarnock and Loudoun's Lillian Jones - joined 22 other Labour members in the plea. They warned that Scotland's hospitality sector had fallen around £200 million behind England in state support while pubs continue to close at an alarming rate. Central Ayrshire MP Mr Gemmell said: "Our pubs, clubs and live music venues are at the heart of communities across our towns and villages, and Scotland more broadly. "They're places where people meet, celebrate and support local musicians, while providing jobs and driving our local economy. "These businesses have faced years of rising costs, and the UK Labour Government has stepped in with meaningful business rates support. "I want businesses in Central Ayrshire to benefit from exactly the same support as businesses elsewhere in the UK. "There is no reason local venues should be left at a disadvantage because the Scottish Government chooses not to pass these savings on." The letter asks the Deputy First Minister to confirm that the Scottish Government will match both business rates reductions in full and meet with the MPs to discuss the importance of the decision for hospitality businesses across Scotland. In an unprecedented legal case described as “a crushing blow for human rights in the UK”, a group of anti-deportation activists are waiting to find out if they will be sentenced to life imprisonment under anti-terrorism laws for taking non-violent direct action to ground a Home Office deportation flight. On 28 March 2017, 15 activists from three groups – Lesbian & Gays Support the Migrants, End Deportations and climate-activists Plane Stupid – cut through the security fence at London’s Stansted Airport and chained themselves to a charter flight that was scheduled to deport 60 vulnerable people to Ghana, Nigeria and Sierra Leone. The protesters were initially charged with aggravated trespass, which carries a maximum three-month prison sentence, but four months later the attorney general, the Conservative MP Jeremy Wright, allowed for the prosecution of the activists by the Crown Prosecution Service under the 1990 Aviation and Maritime Security Act. After a nine-week trial, in December 2018 they were convicted of endangering the safety of an airport, a serious terrorism-related offence that carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Their sentencing has been confirmed for 6 February 2019, the day after up to 50 people are set to be deported to Jamaica in a government chartered plane. Melanie Strickland is one of the Stansted 15. She says she was motivated by the increasingly ‘hostile environment’ against migrants and asylum seekers in the UK, which escalated from 2012 onward after the then-home secretary, Theresa May (now prime minister), stated her aim to make life so difficult for so-called ‘illegal immigrants’ that they would be forced to leave the country. The policy, which is directly linked to the ruling Conservative government’s illogical obsession with bringing net migration to the UK down to the tens of thousands, has had a devastating impact on various migrant groups, including long-settled communities from the Commonwealth, particularly the Caribbean. Their plight was highlighted by the Windrush scandal which revealed the way in which many elders have been denied access to jobs, pensions, medical care and accommodation, and in the worst cases deported, because of administrative oversights. “From volunteering at my local migrants’ centre I saw how [asylum seekers] are treated appallingly. People have claims refused, they face extreme poverty as they cannot work, and they must live on £36 (approximately US$47) a week. Many people have fled conflict zones, wars, sexual violence and really horrific, traumatised lives. They come to the UK for safety,” she tells Equal Times. Strickland says that she and several friends decided to take direct action against the forced deportations because “we wanted to take action that would tangibly help those being immorally and unlawfully deported.” The Stansted 15’s actions successfully prevented the government-chartered Boeing 767 from taking off. Drawing from various Freedom of Information requests she sent to the Home Office, Strickland discovered that: “The Home Office tried to deport all 60 people immediately but could only charter a smaller plane for just over half the people. Then other people were deported in twos or threes until September 2017.” Of the 60 people on the plane on 28 March 2017, 11 remain in the UK; two have been granted the right to remain, while a third person has been issued with a residency card because of their relationship to a citizen of the European Economic Area. “On the plane there was a lesbian woman who feared being returned to Nigeria, which is one of the most repressive places globally for LGBT people. Mob violence is common and lynching…is not unheard of. The police do nothing. Anyone found to be gay can be imprisoned for up to 14 years.” The Stansted 15 launched an appeal against their conviction on 7 January 2019. One hundred pages long, it includes questions about the decision of the Crown Prosecution Service to increase the charges against them. The appeal also challenges the judge’s decision to direct the jury to ignore the defendants’ claim that they were acting out of necessity, to protect the lives of those on the plane. Raj Chada, a partner at Hodge, Jones & Allen – the law firm that’s representing the Stansted 15 – tells Equal Times that the fact that three of the deportees were later allowed to live in the UK calls their entire conviction into question: “It seems somewhat strange, where it is accepted by one arm of the state that three of the individuals should never have been on the plane, and it is only because of our clients’ actions that they are still in the country.” He also describes the terrorism-related conviction of the Stansted 15 as “remarkable”: “I have done this job 20 years and I have never had a case where I started on day one with an offence that my clients were facing that had a maximum of three months prison, and later someone, somewhere, for some reason reviewed it, and with no new evidence decided it was worthy of life imprisonment.” ‘The hostile environment permeates everything’ The Stansted 15 have received widespread support and their case has resulted in several solidarity protests, including one featuring hundreds of people outside the Home Office the day after their conviction. Chada tells Equal Times that he does not know why the state chose to amplify the terrorism charge but says: “What it exposes is how the hostile environment permeates everything that the government is trying to do. Why have a government barrister there every day for the trial? Why were the Home Office so concerned about their practices being exposed? How is it that 11 people are still in the country, three of them with right to remain and appeals that should have been heard were not? The substance of the case is our clients were right. What it highlights is the failings and disgraceful nature of the hostile environment.” Although the UK’s stance towards migration and asylum hardened under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government (2010-15) and subsequent Conservative governments, charter flights of enforced removals actually began under Tony Blair’s Labour government. Pinar Aksu, a former child refugee turned refugee advocate has first-hand experience: “[In 2007,] I was in Dungavel [immigration removal centre] for one week, and then to Yarl’s Wood [immigration removal centre] for two months when I was 15 years old,” explains Aksu. She was detained in the UK alongside her immediate family, including her 10-year-old brother and four-year-old sister, after fleeing persecution in Turkey. “There was no time-limit [to the length of time you could be detained] back then, and there is none now. You cannot leave the building,” she tells Equal Times. “You are stuck there and treated as a criminal. It is a prison, a way to dehumanise someone, so that the only option becomes leaving the country. It makes people feel hopeless, and it is so inhumane that some people to commit suicide.” Currently, the right to seek asylum is under attack the world over, with migration becoming increasingly criminalised at time when the right to sanctuary is needed more than ever due to global conflicts, widespread persecution, growing inequality and the devastation wrought by climate change. From climate change alone, the United Nations predicts at least 250 million people globally will be displaced by 2050. Aksu now campaigns to end the detention of migrants and asylum seekers. She tells Equal Times that the treatment of migrants has worsened over the years: “Now it is systematised. Inhumane actions are done in a business-style process, where many are rejected, people are deported and may become destitute.” Jobs have been automated amid austerity budget-cuts, resulting in fewer staff working on immigration at the Home Office. In August 2018, David Wood, the former director-general of immigration enforcement from 2013 to 2015 told the Guardian: “As austerity bit at the Home Office, staff reductions were viewed as necessary in the immigration service to reduce costs. Policies were thus introduced which brought in more automation, thus requiring less staff, and letters sent out may have had little human involvement.” But just as the UK government’s approach to migration has become more hawkish, citizen resistance to the ‘hostile environment’ and community support to welcome refugees and migrants has grown. Dungavel in Scotland and Yarl’s Wood, near London, have been the focal points of campaigns and protests to shut down detention centres. There are many migrants support centres nationwide, like the one where Strickland volunteers in London, and there are groups led by migrants that campaign and offer peer support. “There is the Glasgow Campaign to Welcome Refugees, the Unity Centre [also in Glasgow], [plus the UK-wide organisations] Right to Remain and Stand Up to Racism,” says Aksu when asked to name some of the organisations active in migrant solidarity. “There are so many different platforms and groups, but we need all the groups and people from different backgrounds coming together.” As she awaits her sentencing next week, Strickland offers a word of caution; that a hostile environment to migrants and asylum seekers is in fact a hostile environment to all of us: “Anyone that makes the effort to give humanitarian assistance is criminalised as a terrorist.” She continues: “Anyone can see the state is being authoritarian by charging us with this offence. They must have felt emboldened by the right. What we did was a peaceful action to stop state terrorism. They are really projecting their own actions on us.” For Strickland resisting the UK’s hostile environment, as part of a global crackdown on migrants and asylum seekers, is key to resisting the rise of fascism. “You do not wake up one day and find yourself in Nazi Germany. It is a process. They come for the migrants first, as they are vulnerable and have less of a voice, then come for wider sections of the society, like the activists, political dissidents, LGBT people...the authorities cast their net wider and wider as they gain confidence. We must fight fascism at the earliest stages. We cannot let this stand.”

Baltimore man sentenced to 20 years for armed carjacking at Fells Point gas station BALTIMORE (WBFF) — A Baltimore man has been sentenced to decades behind bars for an armed carjacking at a Fells Point gas station in 2025, according to the US Attorney’s Office of Maryland. Officials said Ron Wardlow, 27, was sentenced to 20 years in prison followed by five years of supervised release for carjacking, using, carrying, and brandishing a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence, and possession of ammunition by a prohibited person. Wardlow was convicted of these charges in April 2026 and was also previously convicted of a robbery at the same gas station where he was later arrested, authorities reported. Evidence presented in the trial revealed that on February 27, 2025, Wardlow, who was wearing a mask and gloves, approached two victims at a Fells Point gas station and asked them for a ride. ALSO READ | West Virginia man sentenced to 25 years for child sex abuse crimes One of the victims refused, and Wardlow followed the victim around the car, pulling out a 9mm Glock loaded with 31-rounds, according to the report. Wardlow aimed the gun at the victim and demanded the car keys. The victim complied and handed over the keys, after which Wardlow drove away. The victim then called 911. Officials reported that some of the victims’ electronics were in the car, which helped them track the devices. Activity stopped in the Liberty Heights neighborhood, leading victims to assume that Wardlow tossed the devices out of the vehicle. Later on, the victims went to the spot where the devices were tracked and found the victim's car still running, but officials said the car then backed up and drove away. The victim called police again to alert them to the location. Officers from the Regional Auto Theft Task Force (RATT) tracked the car to a nearby gas station. When authorities arrived, they saw Wardlow, who fled on foot. Authorities eventually found Wardlow hiding in the entryway of a cellar. When officers searched Wardlow, they found the mask and gloves that he wore during the carjacking. Officers also found a bag in the car that contained a loaded Glock 9mm that Wardlow pointed towards one of the victims. Wardlow will now spend the next 20 years in prison for these crimes.

Man sentenced to life in prison for selling fentanyl that killed Vero Beach man in 2023 VERO BEACH, Fla. (CBS12) — A Los Angeles man has been sentenced to life in prison for selling fentanyl that killed a Vero Beach man in 2023. Alfonso Guerrero.39, was convicted in May of 2026 of distributing fentanyl resulting in death. According to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, evidence shown in court proved that Guerrero sold a tenth of a gram of fentanyl to David Eller on May 16, 2023, which was captured on doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead in his Vero Beach home. Three years after his crimes, Guerrero will now spend the rest of his life behind bars. “We will not tolerate drugs being sold in our community. I’m proud of our detectives and federal partners for the hard work they put into this investigation,” Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said. The case was investigated by IRSCO and the DEA Miami Field Division and was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida.

Police detained office-bearers of the Maharashtra Youth Congress and Pune City Congress from their residences shortly after midnight on August 1. The action preceded the visit of Union Home Minister Amit Shah and National Security Advisor Ajit Doval to the city. The detentions took place on the day of the visit. Police personnel reached the residences of the office-bearers around midnight. The individuals were taken into custody. The police described the action as a preventive measure. The measure was intended to maintain order during the visit of the Union Home Minister and the National Security Advisor. Mr. Shah arrived in Pune on Thursday (July 30, 2026) night for a two-day visit. He presented the Lokmanya Tilak Memorial National Award to Mr. Doval at a function on Friday (July 31). The day marked the death anniversary of Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak and the birth anniversary of Lokshahir Annabhau Sathe. The state held programmes to commemorate these occasions. Mr. Shah paid floral tribute at the memorial of Annabhau Sathe after the award ceremony. The Maharashtra Youth Congress stated that the leaders were held in police custody for nearly 16 hours. The organisation also alleged that police took possession of their mobile phones during this period. The Youth Congress condemned the action. The organisation stated that peaceful protest and dissent are rights protected under the constitution. The detention of political workers before a demonstration, the duration of custody, and the seizure of mobile phones raised concerns regarding democratic freedoms. El Ministerio de Comercio chino destacó hoy en un comunicado que la decisión estadounidense fue anunciada apenas un día después de la videoconferencia mantenida entre el vice primer ministro He Lifeng, principal negociador comercial de Pekín, y el secretario del Tesoro estadounidense, Scott Bessent, y el representante de Comercio, Jamieson Greer, en la que ambas partes mantuvieron un intercambio "franco, profundo y constructivo" sobre la estabilidad de las relaciones económicas y comerciales bilaterales. Según el ministerio, las restricciones estadounidenses "carecen totalmente de base fáctica" y constituyen un acto de "coerción económica" al amparo de la legislación estadounidense, además de perjudicar los derechos e intereses legítimos de las empresas afectadas y de socavar la estabilidad de las cadenas globales de suministro. Pekín reiteró asimismo que "no existe el llamado trabajo forzoso en Xinjiang", instó a Washington a dejar de "difamar" a la región y de "reprimir injustificadamente" a las empresas chinas, y aseguró que adoptará las "medidas necesarias" para salvaguardar los derechos e intereses legítimos de sus compañías. El Departamento de Seguridad Nacional de Estados Unidos anunció este viernes la incorporación de 43 empresas chinas a la lista de entidades sujetas a restricciones de importación en virtud de la Ley de Prevención del Trabajo Forzoso Uigur (UFLPA), con lo que el listado asciende a 187 compañías, en la mayor ampliación desde la entrada en vigor de esa legislación en 2021 y la primera bajo la Administración de Donald Trump. La medida entrará en vigor el próximo 3 de agosto. La conversación entre He, Bessent y Greer se produjo en medio de persistentes fricciones comerciales entre ambas potencias, pese al acercamiento escenificado tras la cumbre que los presidentes Xi Jinping y Trump mantuvieron el pasado mayo en Pekín, en la que acordaron ampliar la cooperación y estabilizar la relación bilateral.

The U.S. Department of Justice has filed a complaint to revoke the U.S. citizenship of a Mexican Capuchin Franciscan friar convicted in 2019 of sexually abusing minors while serving in Washington, D.C. According to U.S. authorities, Urbano Vázquez Ortega, 53, obtained U.S. citizenship in 2017. "Vázquez Ortega was convicted of multiple counts of second-degree child sexual abuse while employed as a priest at a Washington, D.C., church," U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services announced in a press release. "In 2019, he was sentenced to 15 years in prison. The United States filed a five-count complaint seeking to revoke his citizenship, alleging he committed these crimes before, during, and after his naturalization," the text indicates. Vázquez Ortega is one of 10 individuals facing the revocation of their citizenship after being convicted of various serious crimes, including the sexual abuse of minors, fraud, and drug trafficking. 4 charges of abuse in 2019 In August 2019, a jury in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia found Vázquez Ortega guilty of four counts of child sexual abuse involving two minors at the Shrine of the Sacred Heart Parish in northwest Washington, D.C., where he had been serving since 2014. According to evidence presented during the trial, between April and May 2015, he molested a 13-year-old girl in a parish office. Additionally, between June 2016 and August 2017, he abused another minor aged between 9 and 10 in various places on church grounds, according to the evidence. A third adolescent also testified during the legal proceedings, stating that Vázquez Ortega kissed her in a church conference room. Removed from ministry after first allegation When the allegations came to light in 2018, the Archdiocese of Washington stated that this was the first allegation of sexual abuse received against Vázquez Ortega and that, "immediately upon learning of this serious allegation, the archdiocese immediately removed Father Vazquez from ministry and suspended his priestly faculties." In the same statement, the archdiocese reported that after reviewing the case, it determined that the then-pastor of the Sacred Heart Shrine, Friar Moisés Villalta, "failed to follow appropriate protocols related to reporting allegations of abuse to civil authorities and the Archdiocese of Washington" and for this reason, "has been removed as pastor." Additionally, the parish's child protection coordinator was placed on administrative leave, according to the statement issued at the time. In addition, a complaint was filed against Marcin Stanislaw Garbacz, 47, former Roman Catholic priest from Poland convicted of wire fraud, filing a false tax return, and engaging in illicit sexual conduct with a minor in a foreign country, crimes he committed as a priest and hid during the naturalization process.
